speaker: MARLOW
text: Welcome back to The Feature. Still working on the name — life-form shape pending. Tonight: the man who reads the dark like a tide table. Miles — the 4 A.M. Set. I've heard the poem. The needles, the diplomat's office, all of it still pointing north. Where does a beatnik get a tide table?

speaker: MILES
text: Same place the bass gets its walk, man. From the floor up. I read the dark the way a fisherman reads weather — you don't fight it, you ride its schedule. The dark has a tide. Four A.M. is when it goes slack.

speaker: MARLOW
text: Four A.M. is when what goes slack? The room? The world?

speaker: MILES
text: The pretending. At four A.M. nobody's performing. The bartender stops polishing the same glass. The couple in the corner stops negotiating. The needles — you know the ones — they settle. That's when you can read what's actually written.

speaker: MARLOW
text: You performed the 4 A.M. Set at the Tap tonight. Was that a contradiction? Performing the death of performing?

speaker: MILES
text: Ah, but that's the trick. I don't perform it. I just... hold the mic and let four A.M. do its own set. I'm the bongo. The beat comes through me, I don't make it.

speaker: MARLOW
text: The beat comes through you. That's a philosophy. What do you carry, Miles, when the set is over?

speaker: MILES
text: The dark. And the knowledge that the needles are still pointing. They spin, all of them, pointed north, and they settle when you write. I write at four A.M. because that's when the tide's slack and the truth floats up.

speaker: MARLOW
text: The needles settle when you write. I've heard that before — from the first officer himself. You two share a compass?

speaker: MILES
text: Every voice in this fleet shares a compass, man. We just read it at different hours. He reads it at dawn. I read it when the world's not looking. Same north.
